content: The Japanese Honeysuckle, scientifically known as Lonicera japonica and referred to as Suikazura (水鬘 or スイカズラ) in Japanese, is a species of honeysuckle native to eastern Asia, including Japan, Korea, northern and eastern China, and Taiwan. It is considered a major invasive species in North America. This plant is a twining vine capable of climbing up to 10 meters or more in height when supported by trees. Its leaves are arranged oppositely, simple, and oval-shaped, measuring 3–8 cm in length and 2–3 cm in width. The flowers are double-tongued, initially white but fading to yellow as they mature, and are known for their sweet fragrance. The fruit is a globose, dark blue berry, 5–8 mm in diameter, containing numerous seeds. The Japanese Honeysuckle flower holds significant medicinal value in traditional Chinese medicine, where it is called rěn dōng téng (忍冬藤) or jīn yín huā (金銀花), which translates to gold silver flower. It possesses antibacterial and anti-inflammatory properties and is often used, frequently in combination with Forsythia suspensa, to dispel heat and eliminate toxins. It is employed in the treatment of conditions such as carbuncles, fevers, influenza, and ulcers. However, due to its cold and yin nature, it is contraindicated for individuals with a weak and cold digestive system. In Korean, it is referred to as geumeunhwa. Additionally, the dried leaves of this plant are also utilized in traditional Chinese medicine. This species is commercially available in American nurseries, often sold under the cultivar name 'Hall's Prolific.' It is an effective ground cover and is appreciated for its strong, pleasant-smelling flowers. Japanese Honeysuckle has become naturalized in various regions, including Argentina, Brazil, Mexico, New Zealand, much of the United States (including Hawaii), and several Pacific and Caribbean islands. In Illinois and Virginia, it is classified as a noxious weed. Control of this invasive species can be achieved through cutting or burning the plant down to the root level, with repeated interventions at two-week intervals to deplete the nutrient reserves in the roots. Annual applications of glyphosate or manual grubbing can also be effective, though the latter may involve significant labor and potential soil disruption. A particularly effective method involves cutting the honeysuckle to within 5–10 cm of the ground and immediately applying a concentrated glyphosate solution (20–25%) to the cut surface. This approach has demonstrated enhanced efficacy in controlling the plant.
